newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss economy shrinks again, outlook a bit better.
newsitem.headline: Swiss economy shrinks again, outlook a bit better.

text.p: Switzerland's struggling economy contracted an annualised 0.7 percent in the third quarter of 1996 -- the seventh consecutive quarterly drop -- and officials on Tuesday held out little hope of robust growth in 1997.

Slack demand from consumers scared that their standard of living will fall as unemployment climbs, weak construction activity and a slight decline in exports chopped gross domestic product (GDP) in the period, official statistics showed.
GDP also fell 0.7 percent compared with the year-earlier quarter, the fifth such drop in a row.
Financial markets shrugged off news of the drop, which had leaked out last week and was officially confirmed on Monday.

Investment in equipment by companies trying to boost competitiveness on international markets offered one bright spot in the quarter, rising 9.5 percent, but officials said the overall economy continued to limp along.

"GDP will drop by around 0.75 percent (in 1996) compared with 1995, a year of stagnation, and will not even reach the standard of affluence of 1990," said Commission for Economic Policy chairman Bernd Schips, head of the government's official advisory board.

"In 1997, even with optimistic assumptions for economic development in Europe and the Swiss franc exchange rate and with GDP growth of around 0.5 percent, we will still remain under the level of 1990," he told reporters.
The commision said in a statement it expected 1997 GDP to be driven by export growth due to economic recovery in major global markets, especially in Europe, and a weaker Swiss franc.
"However, these positive impulses contrast with declining domestic demand," the commission said.
It said private consumption would remain little changed and public consumption would fall again next year.

"A particular risk for the development of economic growth is posed by potential turbulance in interest rate or currency exchange rates in connection with the uncertainties of European currency union," the commission said.
The commission forecast unemployment would rise to an annual average rate of 4.75 percent this year and 5.25 percent in 1997.
Both numbers would be records for post-World War Two Switzerland and the highest levels since 4.72 percent in 1994.
"We have to expect that the situation on the labour market will worsen dramatically next year if the proper economic policy decisions are not taken quickly," Schips said.

He called for tax reforms to promote employment, reducing public deficits without cutting investment in crucial areas like education and infrastructure, the elimination of red tape in the bureaucracy and "temporary stagnation of real wages".
The commission listed several reasons for this year's decline and next year's expected slim growth.

Damage to competitiveness from the Swiss franc's strong rise in 1994 and 1995 had still not been repaired. The economy was also hurt by a continuing construction and real estate crisis and structural changes in major sectors.

Demand was crimped by continued pressure for deficit reduction in public budgets and in private households, and the economy was also hit by poor confidence among consumers, employees and some businesses.
It recommended the Swiss National Bank maintain its generous monetary policy until the economy shows clear signs of recovery.
But officials noted the added liquidity was having trouble reaching businesses because banks made averse to risk by the poor economy were building big reserves for bad loans.
